before: Your little one might not be the only one getting accused. When life has gone badly, part of you may try to get some control back by finding someone to blame, like "If you'd gotten it together at fifteen, you could have saved everybody." But figuring out which age of you is to blame doesn't give you what it would have taken back then. That part may start picking on a different age.
after: (Not written yet. The next paragraph, from the guide: instead of asking which version of you deserves blame, ask what that version was trying to do or avoid, what they understood then, what options they could see and stand, what happened because of the choice, what capacity, support or protection was missing, and what you can learn, repair or do differently now. Don't ask those questions here.)
brief:
- the guide: "A five-year-old, an adolescent, a younger adult, and the person you were last year each acted from the awareness, conditioning, fear, support, and options they could actually access then." Carry the point, that every one of those ages could only work with what they actually had then, but don't line up the guide's five things in a row: a five-item list made the last draft read as AI. One or two concrete ones, or the plain gist, is enough.
- the guide: "That does not make every choice harmless. Choices can hurt people, damage a life, and require repair." Keep this: what you actually did can hurt people and damage a life, and the harm can need repair.
- The paragraph before ends on the blaming part's charge, "If you'd gotten it together at fifteen, you could have saved everybody.", and on that part picking on a different age. Answer the charge for every age, the grown-up included: saving everybody was never any age's job. Make it plain that this answers the charge, not what you actually did, which can still need repair.
- the guide: "It means punishment cannot retroactively manufacture the awareness or capacity that was missing." The paragraph before already says that figuring out which age to blame doesn't give you what it would have taken back then. Add the punishment part in a few words only if it says something new; don't repeat that line.
- The article already covers repair ("Your little one was listening, so you go back and apologize to them"); don't explain how to repair here.
length: three to five sentences, 50 to 90 words
guide_passage: A five-year-old, an adolescent, a younger adult, and the person you were last year each acted from the awareness, conditioning, fear, support, and options they could actually access then. That does not make every choice harmless. Choices can hurt people, damage a life, and require repair. It means punishment cannot retroactively manufacture the awareness or capacity that was missing.
next: Instead of asking which version deserves blame, ask: What was that version trying to accomplish or avoid? What did they understand at the time? What options could they actually see and tolerate? What happened because of the choice? What capacity, support, or protection was missing? What can the present adult learn, repair, or do differently now?
